title: Onboarding revamp brainstorm

calendarEvent.title: Onboarding revamp brainstorm
calendarEvent.description:
Whiteboard session for Q4 priority #4 (new-customer onboarding revamp).

Goal: cut new-customer time-to-first-dispatch from ~19 days to under 7.
Format: diverge (sticky notes, no judging), group, dot vote, converge on a top three.

Bring ideas. Working doc: https://docs.google.com/document/d/1Hq3onbRdV2mXk8yPz5LwT0cJ7nB4aS9eF/edit

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, I think it's recording. The little red dot is on, so if anyone says anything embarrassing, it's in the notes forever.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Good to know. Before we start, did anyone else order from the Lebanese place today, or was that just me?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I did. I got the halloumi wrap and the fries were cold again. That's three Thursdays in a row.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: That's because the rider goes all the way around the one-way system. I watched him on the map, he did a full lap of the block.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: We should just do the pizza place downstairs on Thursdays. It's like two minutes away, it would actually arrive hot.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The pizza place gave Diego food poisoning, though.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Diego says that about everywhere. He said it about the sushi place and he still goes there twice a week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I am not having a lunch vendor debate in a meeting we booked for forty-five minutes. Noor, it's your meeting, take it away.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, okay. So, onboarding revamp. This is priority four from Monday's planning, Tom and I own it, and I wanted the four of us in the Blue room with a whiteboard before we commit to anything.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Lena was invited too, but she's at a customer site all afternoon, so she declined. I'll send her the notes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: The problem statement is up on the board. Right now new customers take about nineteen days from contract signed to their first real dispatch in Deino. The goal is to get that under seven.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And just to flag, the nineteen is from memory. It's roughly what we saw in the onboarding review back in July, so it's not a fresh number.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's close enough for today, but we need the real number before we build anything. And what counts as first dispatch, exactly? The first job assigned on the board?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The first job a dispatcher assigns to a real technician, and the technician actually opens it on the mobile app. Not test jobs, and not the ones I create during the kickoff call.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And is the seven calendar days or business days? Because that's a big difference if a customer signs on a Thursday.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Calendar days. It's how the customer experiences it. They don't care that there was a weekend in the middle.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Calendar days, okay. I'm writing that definition in the corner so nobody argues about it later.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So the plan is ten minutes of everybody throwing ideas on sticky notes, no judging. Then we group them, dot vote, and then we argue.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Can I argue now and save us all the time?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: No. Diverge first. Priya, you get a pad too, and you have to write at least three.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Fine. Is there a green pen in here that isn't dead?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: There's a box of them on the windowsill. Tom, before everyone starts writing, can you walk through where the nineteen days actually go? I think it helps to know where the time is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah. So roughly, the first few days are the kickoff call and getting their technician list. They send me a spreadsheet, usually a messy one, and I clean it up in Google Sheets and run the import script.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Then the big one is calendars. Every technician has to click a connect-calendar link and do the OAuth flow themselves. With Fernhollow it was eleven days just waiting for technicians to click that link.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Eleven days just on the calendar link?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Eleven days. Owen was literally walking around the depot with a tablet getting people to log in. Some of the older techs had never logged into their work Google account at all.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And then the last bit is the dispatchers learning the board and setting up job types, durations, skills, all of that. That part depends a lot on how organized they are.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So it's data in, calendar connections, and then people learning the product. That's a useful split. Okay, go, sticky notes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: I've got one. CSV import, but self-serve. The customer uploads their technicians and their open jobs and maps the columns themselves, instead of Tom running a script.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I literally wrote the same one. CSV import of technicians and jobs. Mine has a smiley face on it though.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Put them on top of each other. Okay, mine are a guided setup checklist, like a progress bar in the app with the steps you need before your first dispatch. And a sample-data sandbox.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: What's the sandbox exactly, in your head?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: A fake company that's already set up, with twenty technicians and a week of jobs. So the dispatchers can play with the board on day one without breaking anything real.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: They learn the product while Tom is still importing their actual data, instead of waiting.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Separate tenant, I assume? Not mixed into their real account?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Separate tenant, yeah. It gets wiped every night. Okay, next.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Mine is connecting calendars in bulk with admin consent. On Microsoft 365, a tenant admin can grant consent for the whole organization in one click, and on Google Workspace the equivalent is domain-wide delegation.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So instead of chasing sixty technicians to click a link, the customer's IT person does it once and we're done. That kills Tom's eleven days.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Oh, that would be huge. Okay, mine is a white-glove week. For the first week after kickoff I basically live in their account, I build their job types, and I sit with the dispatchers on a call every morning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So like a concierge.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Like a concierge, yeah. I know it doesn't scale, I can maybe do two a month, but I wanted it on the board.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The two customers where I basically did that by accident last spring both dispatched in under a week. So I know it works, it just costs me.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: It works because it's you, though. That's not a product, that's a Tom.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: No judging. Okay, I also have video walkthroughs. Short ones, two minutes each, embedded in the app next to each step.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And somebody, I think it was me, also wrote in-app chat widget. Like the little bubble in the bottom corner.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And mine is templates per trade. HVAC, plumbing, electrical. When you sign up you pick your trade and you get job types, typical durations, and skill tags already filled in.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Oh, that's good, because I build basically the same HVAC job types every single time. Annual service, no-heat call, install, warranty visit.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Wait, so are templates their own thing, or part of the checklist? Because I could see them being...

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Their own thing for now. We group them in a minute.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Also one more, which is more of a question than an idea. Does the sandbox and the import have to...

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Sorry, sorry, go ahead.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: No, it's fine, I'll save it for when we get to the CSV stuff. It's a security thing.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Ooh, that sounds ominous.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Tom, I'm sorry, but I can't read half of your sticky notes. Is that one white-glove or white goods?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: White-glove. My handwriting is fine, it's the pen.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, I think the board's pretty full, so let me group them. Over here is data in, so CSV import, templates per trade, and sort of the sandbox.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Then connections, which is just the admin consent one. And then guidance, which is the checklist, the videos, the chat widget, and Tom's white-glove week.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That grouping matches Tom's three buckets almost exactly, which is nice. Data, calendars, learning.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, before we vote, does anyone want to kill something? This is the part where Priya gets to argue.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'll kill one of my own, the chat widget. I'm one support engineer. If we put a chat bubble in the app, I'm the only one behind it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I'd be answering chats at nine p.m. from dispatchers in three time zones.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And since the sync bug hit, our ticket volume is up about forty percent. I just can't take on another channel right now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: But wouldn't it catch people when they're stuck, before they give up?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: It would, and then they'd be stuck waiting for me instead. A chat widget with nobody behind it is worse than no chat widget.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah, I agree. The support load is the problem. Let's cross it off, and if the checklist works, people should be getting stuck less anyway.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, crossed off. Sad face, but crossed off.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: What about the videos? They're cheap.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: They're cheap to make once. The problem is every time we change the UI they're wrong, and nobody ever remembers to re-record them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The Fernhollow dispatchers did love the Loom I made them last year, though. Maybe someone could record a few at some point.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Maybe. Let's not vote on it as a project, though. Videos aren't going to move nineteen days to seven.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And the sandbox, I mean, I like it, but it's a whole second tenant with fake data that has to look realistic. Someone has to maintain that seed data forever.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's fair. It's more of a nice to have.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I'd say the same about it. It helps dispatchers learn, but the learning part isn't where most of the nineteen days go. The calendar part is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, dot voting. Everyone gets three dots, and you can stack them on one idea if you really care. Go.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Can I put a dot on the chat widget being crossed off?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: No. Three dots, real ideas only.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, is everyone done? Noor, do you want to count?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, so CSV import has four dots, so everyone. The setup checklist has three, admin-consent calendar connect has three. Templates per trade has one and the sandbox has one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And the white-glove week has zero, which is honestly fair. I didn't even vote for it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: That's twelve dots, four people times three. The math works.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So the top three are CSV import, the setup checklist, and admin-consent calendar connect. Which, I mean, is basically one per bucket.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: I like that. And templates and the sandbox aren't dead, they're just not this quarter. Templates might even fold into the checklist later as a step.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Can I lobby for templates for one second? Every HVAC customer, I spend most of an afternoon building the same job types.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Honestly, a template is just a seed file. HVAC job types, durations, skill tags. That's not a big project.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: If Noor's checklist has a job types step, a start-from-HVAC button there might be a day of work. But I don't want to promise it today, let's see the mockups first.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I'll leave space for it in the design. No promises.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Can I also be the skeptic for a minute? Even with all three of these, I don't believe we hit seven days while calendars are still manual until December.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, I was going to say. Calendars alone were eleven days at Fernhollow.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's fair. So seven is the target once admin consent ships. For customers we onboard in October and November, the target is ten days, and we hold ourselves to that.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Ten as the interim target, seven as the real one. I'm writing that under the goal.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Okay. That I believe.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, so now we converge, one at a time. Checklist first, because it's mine and I'm biased.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: My rough version is six steps. Company profile, import technicians, connect calendars, set up job types, invite dispatchers, and then create and dispatch your first job.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Each one checks itself off automatically when you actually do the thing. No manual ticking.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Can calendars be step two instead of three? It's the long pole. I'd rather start that clock on day one while they're still fiddling with their technician list.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: But you can't connect calendars for technicians who don't exist yet.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Okay, true. But the admin can at least send the invites as soon as each technician is imported, not wait for the whole list.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: That's a good point. So the steps are ordered, but they can overlap. I'll show that in the mockup.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Can I have an internal view of that? Like a list of every new customer and which step they're stuck on. Right now I find out someone's stuck when Lena forwards me an angry email.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Oh, yes. That's actually maybe the more valuable half.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Agree. The customer sees a checklist, Tom sees a funnel. And step six is literally our metric, so we get time to first dispatch measured for free.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Where does the state live? Per account or per user?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Per account, I think. If two admins are setting it up, they should both see the same progress.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Per account is right. Can steps be skipped? Like if a customer doesn't want to connect calendars on day one?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I'd let them skip and come back. A skipped step stays visible, it just doesn't block the next one.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And then maybe an email nudge if someone's stuck on a step for more than three days?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Maybe, later. Let's get the basic thing right first.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay. Noor, when can you have something we can look at?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: I can have mockups of the checklist and Tom's internal view by Thursday next week, so the eighth.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Great. Okay, admin consent. Let me talk this one through, because it's the most technical of the three.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: On the Microsoft side, it's an application permission for calendars, and the admin grants it once for the whole tenant. On Google, the admin goes into the Workspace admin console and pastes in our client ID and the calendar scopes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Okay, but my worry there is scope. App-level access on Microsoft means we can read every calendar in their tenant, not just the technicians. The CFO's calendar, the HR person's calendar, everything.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Right. On Microsoft you can restrict it with an application access policy, scoped to a security group. So the customer makes a technicians group, and we only ever see those mailboxes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And what about on Google?

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Google is harder. Domain-wide delegation isn't group-scoped, so we'd have to enforce it ourselves and only ever impersonate users who are on the technician list.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Then I want that enforced in exactly one place in the code, with an audit log, not sprinkled around. And it has to be in SOC 2 scope, because the observation window starts on the first of November.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's fair. The other problem is who builds it, because this sits right next to Calendar Sync v2 and Maya is heads down on that. And frankly, she's exhausted after the duplicate jobs mess.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah, she's been on call for like two weeks straight.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So I don't want to put any of this on Maya until after the v2 beta on the thirteenth of November. We design it now, and we build it after the beta, on top of the webhook work.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So it's in the top three, but it ships last.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: It ships last. Which is fine, honestly. The checklist and the import can go first, and they don't depend on sync at all.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: And for the next couple of months I'll keep chasing calendar links by hand. At least I've got a script for the reminder emails now.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Oh, and what about customers whose technicians use personal Gmail? We've got a few small ones like that, no Workspace at all.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Then admin consent doesn't apply and they fall back to the per-technician link. That's fine, those are usually the small accounts with ten technicians, not sixty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Hang on, I want to pull up the onboarding doc so I can add this, and the wifi just dropped again.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: The Blue room wifi is cursed. It's been like this since we moved in.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: It's the access point in the ceiling. It's the old one from the previous tenant, and it can't handle more than about six devices. I keep meaning to swap it out.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Is that a real fix or a someday fix?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Someday fix. Maybe I'll look at it next week if I have a spare hour, no promises.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Can we just buy one of those mesh things? They're like a hundred and fifty dollars.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Not in this meeting. Put it in the office channel and Aisha can decide whether the landlord pays for it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay, I'm on my phone hotspot now. Got it. Carry on.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So, CSV import. Tom, do you want to describe the current pain?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: So today the customer emails me a spreadsheet. Sometimes it's an Excel file with six tabs. I clean it up in Google Sheets, I fix the phone numbers, I run Maya's old import script, and it takes me most of a day per customer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And the vision is they upload it themselves, we show a preview, they map columns like name, email, phone, skills, home depot, and then they hit import. I was thinking we'd parse it in the browser so the preview is instant.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Okay, so this is my security thing. Can I do it now?

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Yes. Now you can argue.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Three things. First, PII. A technician file has names, personal phone numbers, often home addresses because they start the day from home.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And people put weird stuff in extra columns. I've seen driver's license numbers in a notes column. Somebody once sent us a column called emergency contact with people's mothers' phone numbers in it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And jobs are worse, because jobs have the end customers' addresses and phone numbers and sometimes gate codes. That's not even our customer's data, it's their customers' data.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Gate codes, yeah. And alarm codes. Fernhollow had alarm codes in their job notes.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Right. Second, size, because if the upload is unbounded, somebody uploads a two hundred megabyte export from their old system and the parser falls over. Or worse, it takes the whole API down with it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And third, formula injection. If someone puts a cell that starts with an equals sign, or a plus or minus or an at sign, and later a dispatcher exports the job list and opens it in Excel, that formula runs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Something like a HYPERLINK formula that sends data somewhere when you click it. It's an old trick, but it still works.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Sorry, give me a concrete example. Like what would someone actually type?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: A technician name cell that says equals HYPERLINK, some attacker's URL, and then click here. The dispatcher exports their roster, opens it in Excel, clicks it, and the neighbouring cells go along for the ride.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Wait, so is that a problem with our export or with our import?

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Both sides. The import is how the poison gets in, and the export is where it goes off. So we treat every imported value as hostile, and we escape anything that starts with those characters when we export.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Okay, that's a really good catch. And honestly, the current process is worse than anything we'd build. We have technician spreadsheets sitting in Tom's inbox and in a shared Google Drive folder.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah. Several of them. I should probably clean that up at some point.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Before the first of November would be nice. Just saying.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: I hear you. I'll look at it, it's mostly old stuff from last year.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: That's exactly what the auditors from Kestrel will ask about. Where does customer PII live, and who can see it.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So what does this change? Let me propose something, and you tell me if it's wrong.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: One, we parse server-side, streaming, not in the browser, with a hard cap. Two, only allow-listed columns get imported, and anything else is dropped and never stored, so there's no free-text notes column in v1.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Three, the raw uploaded file is deleted after twenty-four hours. Nobody emails spreadsheets to Tom anymore once this ships.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: What's the hard cap, though?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Our biggest customer has, what, three hundred technicians? And even Brightkite would be about two hundred and twenty.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: So five thousand rows and five megabytes per file is really generous for technicians.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Five thousand rows, five megabytes, I can live with that. And CSV only, no Excel files, because an xlsx is basically a zip and I don't want to deal with zip bombs.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: People are going to send Excel files, though. Like, all of them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: They will, but saving as CSV is something I can walk them through. It's one click in Excel.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And four, escape on export. A leading single quote on anything that starts with equals, plus, minus, or at. That one's cheap, and we should do it regardless of the importer.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Can I still do the preview, though? The preview is kind of the whole UX.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah. The server parses the first fifty rows and sends back a preview, and the user maps the columns on that. It's a bit slower than parsing in the browser, but it's fine.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Okay. That's fine. I can design around a one-second spinner.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: What happens when they re-upload the file with fixes? Half my time today is re-running the script because they sent me a corrected version.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Match on email. If the technician exists, we update them, and we never delete anyone from an import. Deleting stays a manual action in the app.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: And every import gets logged, who uploaded it, when, and how many rows were created or updated. Not the contents, just the counts.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: One more thing, I'd split it. Technicians first, jobs later. Technicians are the bottleneck Tom described, and the jobs data is the scarier PII.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Honestly, most customers' open jobs are only a week or two out anyway. They can create those by hand, or I can help them.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Yeah, I agree with that. So CSV import v1 is technicians only, and jobs import waits until Priya's done the threat model and we've decided how to handle the end-customer data.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: So that changes my mockups a bit. The import screen is technicians only, and I drop the jobs tab.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Right, and it changes the order of work. Priya, can you write up threat-model notes for the CSV import, even rough ones? I want them before we finalize anything.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4
segments.text: Yeah. I'll write up the threat-model notes for the CSV import and have them in the onboarding doc by Friday the ninth.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Perfect. Okay, before we wrap, I want to come back to the nineteen days.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: Tom, can you pull actual time-to-first-dispatch numbers for the last ten customers we onboarded? Contract date to first real dispatch, using the definition on the board.

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Yeah. I can get that from the admin panel plus the contract dates in the CRM. I'll have the last ten customers' numbers by Monday.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: Can you split it by the three buckets? Like how many days in data, how many in calendars, how many in learning?

segments.speaker: Speaker 2
segments.text: Where I can, yeah. The calendar part is easy to see in the logs, the rest is fuzzier. I'll do my best.

segments.speaker: Speaker 1
segments.text: That's great. If it turns out it's actually twenty-five days, or twelve, that changes how ambitious the seven is.

segments.speaker: Speaker 3
segments.text: And I'll put the baseline on the first slide of the review, so we're all looking at the same number.

segments.speaker: Speaker 4

decisions: The top three onboarding ideas from the dot vote are CSV import, a guided setup checklist (with an internal stuck-customer view for Tom), and admin-consent bulk calendar connect.
The in-app chat widget is rejected because of the support load it would put on Tom.
CSV import v1 covers technicians only; job import waits until Priya's threat model is done.

Admin-consent calendar connect is designed now but built only after the Calendar Sync v2 beta (13 November), without pulling in Maya before then.
Templates per trade and the sample-data sandbox are parked for later, not built this quarter.
Interim target of 10 days to first dispatch for customers onboarded in October and November; 7 days is the target once admin-consent connect ships.
The under-seven-days target is measured in calendar days.
